greek: Καὶ συνετελέσθησαν ὁ οὐρανὸς καὶ ἡ γῆ καὶ πᾶς ὁ κόσμος αὐτῶν.
hint: The last sentence of the making, and the first of the resting.

notes.text: Aorist passive indicative, 3rd plural, of συντελέω — συν- + τελέω, to bring a thing *quite* to its end. Passive: the heaven and the earth are not finishing, they are finished. The lexicon's range runs on to *make up the whole* and *make up the number*, a sense of completing a count, which is why the chain keeps both.

Middle Liddell's first sense is *order* — arrangement, good order, and from there the *adornment* that gives English *cosmetic*. The sense *world* is late and is not the first. [[flag]] Hebrew *ṣĕbāʾām* is *their host*, an army: the sun, moon and stars as ranked troops. The Greek keeps the ranking and loses the soldiers.
*All, the whole* — the whole of a thing taken together, not merely each of its parts. With κόσμος it is the ordered array entire.
None in this verse.

reading: And [[were brought quite to an end|were brought quite to an end, were completed, were accomplished, were made up into the whole and into the number]] — one completed act seen whole, not a process observed in progress — [[the heaven|the vaulted arch, the sky-expanse, the region above and over]] and [[the earth|the land, the dry ground, the soil, the territory, the terrestrial realm as the counterpart-below]] and [[all|all, the whole, every, every single]] [[the order|the order, the good order and decency, the form and fashion, the government, the ornament and adornment]] of them.

greek: καὶ συνετέλεσεν ὁ θεὸς ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ ἕκτῃ τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ, ἃ ἐποίησεν, καὶ κατέπαυσεν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ ἑβδόμῃ ἀπὸ πάντων τῶν ἔργων αὐτοῦ, ὧν ἐποίησεν.
hint: The number in this verse is not the number the Hebrew has.

notes.text: The Greek reads *on the sixth day* where the Hebrew reads *on the seventh*. [[flag]] The Hebrew has God finishing on the seventh day and resting on it, which reads as though the finishing were itself work done on the sabbath; the Greek removes the difficulty by moving the finishing back a day. The Samaritan Pentateuch and the Syriac agree with the Greek. This is a decision made by translators, and it is visible only if the Greek is read as the text rather than corrected toward the Hebrew.

Aorist of καταπαύω, whose first sense is transitive — *to lay to rest, put an end to*, something done *to* a thing — and whose range runs through *make to cease*, *hinder*, *check*, as far as *kill*. English *rested* is intransitive and carries none of that. Hebrew *šābat* is simply *ceased*, and gives the sabbath its name.
ἀπό with the genitive: separation, *away from*. The resting is not inactivity but a standing apart from the works.
Neuter plural relatives, accusative then genitive: *which he made* both times, the case changing with the verb that governs it, not the sense. English cannot show the difference.
None in this verse.

reading: And [[brought quite to an end|brought quite to an end, completed, accomplished, made up into the whole and into the number]] — one completed act seen whole, not a process observed in progress — [[the God|he who is God definitively, the one the article marks out, the known and the only]] [[in the day|within, inside of, and by means of the day, the day-break, the time]] the sixth [[the works|the works, the business, the deeds, the action, the works of industry and the tilled lands]] of him, which [[made|fashioned, wrought, manufactured, produced, performed, and brought to a finished and accomplished state]], and [[laid to rest|laid to rest, put an end to, made to cease, stopped and kept in check, put down]] [[the day|the day, the day-break, the time]] the seventh [[from|from, away from, far from, apart from]] [[all|all, the whole, every, every single]] [[the works|the works, the business, the deeds]] of him, which [[made|fashioned, wrought, produced]].

greek: καὶ ηὐλόγησεν ὁ θεὸς τὴν ἡμέραν τὴν ἑβδόμην καὶ ἡγίασεν αὐτήν, ὅτι ἐν αὐτῇ κατέπαυσεν ἀπὸ πάντων τῶν ἔργων αὐτοῦ, ὧν ἤρξατο ὁ θεὸς ποιῆσαι.
hint: Three verbs, and the third gives the reason for the first two.

notes.text: εὐλογέω, εὖ + λόγος: *to speak well of*. That is the lexicon's first sense, and *to bless* is its fourth. The English word *bless* has drifted so far toward benefaction that the speaking has fallen out of it; the Greek is an act of good speech before it is anything else. Augmented ηὐ- rather than εὐ-, as Rahlfs prints it.

ἁγιάζω has no entry in Middle Liddell at all — it is a word the Septuagint and the New Testament use and the classical language largely does not. LSJ gives it no gloss of its own either: the entry reads *= ἁγίζω*, and cites this verse. So the sense is ἁγίζω's, *hallow, make sacred*.

The lexicon prints two entries under this spelling: ὅ τι, *for what, wherefore*, and the conjunction, *that*. This is the second. Its range covers both the *that* of reported speech and the *because* the sense requires here, and the chain holds them together rather than choosing.

Aorist middle of ἄρχω. Perseus opens the entry with *in pass. sense:— to be first*, a gloss belonging to the passive alone; the first numbered sense, marked "both in Act. and Mid.", is *to begin, make a beginning*, and that is this form. With the infinitive ποιῆσαι: *began to make*.
*Which God began to make.* The Hebrew has *which God created to make* — ʾăšer bārāʾ laʿăśôt, a notoriously hard phrase. The Greek resolves it into a beginning, which the Hebrew does not say.
None in this verse.

reading: And [[spoke well of|spoke well of, praised, honoured, blessed]] — one completed act seen whole, not a process observed in progress — [[the God|he who is God definitively, the one the article marks out, the known and the only]] [[the day|the day, the day-break, the time]] the seventh and [[hallowed|hallowed, made sacred]] it, [[that|that, seeing that, although, for that, because, inasmuch as]] [[in it|within, inside of, and by means of it]] [[laid to rest|laid to rest, put an end to, made to cease]] [[from|from, away from, far from, apart from]] [[all|all, the whole, every, every single]] [[the works|the works, the business, the deeds]] of him, which [[began|began, made a beginning, made a beginning of, began from]] [[the God|he who is God definitively, the one the article marks out]] [[to make|to make, to do, to produce, to create]].

greek: Αὕτη ἡ βίβλος γενέσεως οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς, ὅτε ἐγένετο, ᾗ ἡμέρᾳ ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν
hint: The verse the whole book is named from, and it does not end.

notes.text: Middle Liddell's first sense is *the inner bark of the papyrus* — the material, before anything is written on it. *A book* is its third. The headword takes the first sense, which is why this reads as it does: the rule is the lexicon's order, not the expected word, and the seam is left showing.

γένεσις: *an origin, source, productive cause*. The book's Greek title, and the word this verse gives it. Genitive, anarthrous. It holds together the origin of a thing and the account of that origin, which English splits into *genesis* and *generations*.
γίνομαι again, against the εἰμί of 1:2 — *came to be*, not *was*. Singular, though its subject is heaven and earth together.

John 1:19, the first verse after the prologue, is built the same way: αὕτη ἐστὶν ἡ μαρτυρία τοῦ Ἰωάννου ὅτε ἀπέστειλαν. A demonstrative, a noun with its genitive, and ὅτε bringing in the occasion; where Genesis has no verb, John supplies ἐστίν. John's prologue has already opened with Genesis's first two words, Ἐν ἀρχῇ. Whether this heading is meant to be heard again the grammar cannot say; that the two are built alike, it can.
Dative of time without a preposition: *on which day*. The relative pronoun is the only marker, and English has to supply a preposition the Greek does not print.

The verse ends here with no stop: Rahlfs prints τὴν γῆν and runs straight into καὶ πᾶν χλωρόν in verse 5, one sentence across the verse division. The reading text ends unpunctuated for the same reason.
None in this verse.

reading: [[this|this, the nearer, what follows]] [[the inner bark of the papyrus|the inner bark of the papyrus, the bark, the book]] [[of origin|of origin, of source, of productive cause, of beginning, of manner of birth, of race and descent, of production and generation, of creation and the created things]] [[of heaven|of heaven, of the vault, of the firmament and the sky]] and [[of earth|of earth, of land, of the ground]], [[when|when, sometimes]] [[came into being|there came to be, there arose, there was brought into existence]], in which [[day|the day, the day-break, the time]] [[made|fashioned, wrought, manufactured, produced, performed, and brought to a finished and accomplished state]] [[the God|he who is God definitively, the one the article marks out, the known and the only]] [[the heaven|the vaulted arch, the sky-expanse, the region above and over]] and [[the earth|the land, the dry ground, the soil, the territory, the terrestrial realm as the counterpart-below]]

greek: καὶ πᾶν χλωρὸν ἀγροῦ πρὸ τοῦ γενέσθαι ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς καὶ πάντα χόρτον ἀγροῦ πρὸ τοῦ ἀνατεῖλαι· οὐ γὰρ ἔβρεξεν ὁ θεὸς ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν, καὶ ἄνθρωπος οὐκ ἦν ἐργάζεσθαι τὴν γῆν,
hint: The sentence that began in verse 4 is still running, and still has not stopped.

notes.text: χλωρός is a colour before it is a plant: *greenish-yellow*, the shade of new growth, of honey, of sand, of a face gone pale. The green thing is named from the colour, not the colour from the thing, and the lexicon's order keeps it that way.

Middle Liddell's first sense is *an inclosed place, a feeding-place* — the fenced ground, before the fodder standing in it. *Grass* is its fourth. English has no word that is both the pasture and what grows there, so the headword reads as the enclosure and the chain carries the rest.

πρό with the articular infinitive, twice: *before the coming-to-be*, *before the rising-up*. Greek can make a verb into a noun and keep it a verb; English must choose, and loses the action in choosing.

βρέχω, with ὁ θεός as its subject: God had not rained. Every gloss Perseus tags in the entry's first sense sits inside its *:—Pass.* clause — *to be wetted, get wet* — while that sense's own active, *to wet* (Lat. *rigo*), it never tags; the second sense, *to rain, send rain*, it marks as New Testament usage, and that is this form.
εἰμί with the infinitive: *there was not a man to work it*. The imperfect holds the absence open across the whole stretch of time rather than reporting it once.
None in this verse.

reading: and [[all|all, the whole, every, every single]] [[greenish-yellow|greenish-yellow, pale-green, light-green, green and grassy, yellow, pale and bleached, fresh and living]] [[of field|of field, of lands, of a farm, of the country]] [[before|before, in front of, further on, sooner, rather than]] [[to come into being|to come to be, to arise, to be brought into existence]] [[upon|upon, on, in, at, near]] [[the earth|the land, the dry ground, the terrestrial realm]] and [[all|all, the whole, every, every single]] [[an inclosed place|an inclosed place, a feeding-place, any feeding-ground, food and fodder and provender, grass, hay]] [[of field|of field, of lands, of a farm, of the country]] [[before|before, in front of, further on, sooner, rather than]] [[to make to rise up|to make to rise up, to grow up, to give birth to and bring to light, to rise, to take its rise, to grow]]; for not [[rained|rained, sent rain]] [[the God|he who is God definitively, the one the article marks out, the known and the only]] [[upon|upon, on, in, at, near]] [[the earth|the land, the dry ground, the terrestrial realm]], and [[man|a man, a human being]] was not, and kept on not being, [[to work|to work, to labour, to work at and make and build, to do and perform and accomplish, to work the land, to earn by working]] [[the earth|the land, the dry ground, the terrestrial realm]],

greek: πηγὴ δὲ ἀνέβαινεν ἐκ τῆς γῆς καὶ ἐπότιζεν πᾶν τὸ πρόσωπον τῆς γῆς.
hint: One Greek word for what waters the ground, and nobody is certain what the Hebrew one means.

notes.text: Hebrew *ʾēd* occurs twice in the whole Bible and its sense is not settled — *mist*, *stream*, or a flood-word borrowed from Akkadian *edû*. [[flag]] The Greek does not hedge: πηγή, a spring, water rising from below rather than falling from above. A translator's decision stands where the Hebrew leaves a question.

Middle Liddell marks its first sense *mostly in pl.*, and prints it *running waters, streams*; the text has the singular. The headword keeps the lexicon's first translation as the rule requires, and the number is recorded here instead.
Two imperfects: the spring kept going up and kept watering. Against the aorists of verses 1–3, which see an act whole, these hold the action open.

Here the Greek *does* render the Hebrew's *face* — πρόσωπον for *pĕnê hāʾădāmâ* — where at both points of 1:2 it dropped it. The difference is the Septuagint's own, and it is why *face of the waters* must never be written back into that verse while *the face of the earth* stands correctly in this one.
None in this verse.

reading: [[but|but, however, whereas, on the other hand]], [[running waters|running waters, streams, a fount, a source, an origin]] [[was going up|was going up, was mounting, was going up to, was embarking]] [[out of|out of, forth from, from]] [[the earth|the land, the dry ground, the terrestrial realm]] and [[was giving to drink|was giving to drink, was watering, was watering the cattle]] [[all|all, the whole, every, every single]] [[the face|the face, the visage, the countenance, the look, the mask, the outward appearance]] [[of the earth|of the land, of the dry ground, of the terrestrial realm]].

greek: καὶ ἔπλασεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν ἄνθρωπον χοῦν ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς καὶ ἐνεφύσησεν εἰς τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ πνοὴν ζωῆς, καὶ ἐγένετο ὁ ἄνθρωπος εἰς ψυχὴν ζῶσαν.
hint: Two words for breath in one verse, and neither of them is πνεῦμα.

notes.text: πλάσσω is the potter's verb, Latin *fingere*: to work clay or wax into a shape. It gives English *plastic* and *plasma*. Not the ἐποίησεν of chapter 1, and not a word used of the heaven and the earth.

The lexicon prints two entries under this spelling: a liquid measure, the Pitcher-feast, and this one — *earth thrown down, heaped up, dust*. The second is the word here. Double accusative: the man is formed, and dust is what he is formed as.

Middle Liddell gives ἐμφυσάω one gloss, *to blow in: to play the flute*, where the colon marks a special application of the verb rather than a second sense of it. The verb is *blow in*; the flute is what blowing in amounts to in Aristophanes. The chain carries both because the lexicon does.

πνοή's first sense is *a blowing* — the same first sense the lexicon gives πνεῦμα at 1:2. The two words for moving air stand in the same book with the same opening gloss, and neither is *spirit* first.

εἰς of result: the man came to be *into* something. And ψυχή's first sense in Middle Liddell is *breath* — so the phrase runs breath into breath: God blows in a blowing, and the man becomes a living breath. English *soul* arrives only later in the entry and brings a whole anthropology with it that the Greek word does not carry here.

The same phrase the Greek uses of the sea creatures and the beasts in 1:20, 1:24 and again at 2:19. It is not said of the man alone, and a version that renders it *living soul* here and *living creature* there has decided something the Greek does not.
None in this verse.

reading: and [[formed|formed, moulded, shaped, moulded and formed by training, formed in the mind, put into a certain form]] — one completed act seen whole, not a process observed in progress — [[the God|he who is God definitively, the one the article marks out, the known and the only]] [[the man|the man, the human being, mankind]] [[earth thrown down|earth thrown down, heaped up, dust]] [[from|from, away from, far from, apart from]] [[the earth|the land, the dry ground, the terrestrial realm]] and [[blew in|blew in, played the flute]] [[into|into, to, in, rest in]] [[the face|the face, the visage, the countenance, the look, the outward appearance]] of him [[a blowing|a blowing, a blast, a breeze, a breathing hard, breath, flame]] [[of a living|of a living, of the means of life and substance, of life and existence, of a way of life]], and [[came into being|there came to be, there arose, there was brought into existence]] [[the man|the man, the human being, mankind]] [[into|into, to, in, rest in]] [[breath|breath, the life, the spirit, life and death, the ghost, the departed soul]] [[living|living, alive, in full life and strength, fresh, strong]].

greek: Καὶ ἐφύτευσεν κύριος ὁ θεὸς παράδεισον ἐν Εδεμ κατὰ ἀνατολὰς καὶ ἔθετο ἐκεῖ τὸν ἄνθρωπον, ὃν ἔπλασεν.
hint: The first κύριος in the book, and the lexicon's second sense for παράδεισος names this very garden.

notes.text: The first occurrence in this project. Middle Liddell opens the entry as an adjective, *having power*; the first noun sense is *authority over, lord*, and the rule takes the first noun sense. Anarthrous here. It renders the Hebrew divine name, which the Greek does not transliterate but replaces with a title — a substitution made by the translators and invisible in English versions that print LORD.

A Persian loanword, *pairidaēza*, a walled enclosure. Middle Liddell's first sense is *a park*; its second is *the garden of Eden, Paradise* — the lexicon naming this passage as the source of the English word. Anarthrous: *a park*, not *the*.

κατά's first sense is *down, downwards*, and the entry heads all three cases together, so the case cannot be read off it. The idiom κατὰ ἀνατολάς means *eastward*; ἀνατολή is *a rising*, and the east is where the rising happens. The reading gives the lexicon's senses and the idiom is recorded here.
Aorist middle of τίθημι, *to set, put, place*. The middle carries an interest of the subject's own that English cannot mark.

Transliterated, not translated: the Greek keeps the Hebrew *ʿĒden*, a word for luxury or delight. Whether it is the place-name or the common noun is exactly what the transliteration refuses to decide.

reading: And [[planted|planted, planted for himself, begot, produced and brought about and caused]] — one completed act seen whole, not a process observed in progress — [[lord|lord, master, the one having power and authority over]] [[the God|he who is God definitively, the one the article marks out, the known and the only]] [[a park|a park, the garden of Eden, paradise]] in [[name:Εδεμ]] [[down|down, downwards, down from, down upon, over, upon]] [[risings|risings, rises, the quarter of sunrise, the east]] and [[set|set, put, placed, planted, laid]] [[there|there, in that place]] [[the man|the man, the human being, mankind]], whom [[formed|formed, moulded, shaped, put into a certain form]].

greek: καὶ ἐξανέτειλεν ὁ θεὸς ἔτι ἐκ τῆς γῆς πᾶν ξύλον ὡραῖον εἰς ὅρασιν καὶ καλὸν εἰς βρῶσιν καὶ τὸ ξύλον τῆς ζωῆς ἐν μέσῳ τῷ παραδείσῳ καὶ τὸ ξύλον τοῦ εἰδέναι γνωστὸν καλοῦ καὶ πονηροῦ.
hint: The tree is ξύλον — wood, timber, a plank — and the same word will carry a cross.

notes.text: Not δένδρον, the living tree, but ξύλον: *wood*, cut timber, a piece of wood, a post, a cudgel. The Greek of this chapter names the material rather than the plant, and the same word stands in Acts 5:30 and Galatians 3:13 for the cross.

Middle Liddell gives ἐξανατέλλω a single sense, *to spring up from*, intransitive, while the LXX uses it here transitively, with God as subject: he made to spring up. With one gloss there is no range to open, so it stands as plain text in both panels and the transitive use is recorded here.

βρῶσις opens at *meat* and goes on to *eating* and, third, *corrosion, rust* — the same range Matthew 6:19 uses of what destroys treasure. The tree is good for the eating of it, which is what the chain keeps.

notes.lemma: τοῦ εἰδέναι γνωστὸν καλοῦ καὶ πονηροῦ
notes.text: Word for word: *the wood of the to-know knowable of beautiful and of toilsome*. [[flag]] The Greek adds γνωστόν, *known* or *knowable*, which the Hebrew does not have — *ʿēṣ hadda'at ṭôb wārāʿ* is simply the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. And πονηρός's first sense is *toilsome, painful, grievous*: the word for evil begins as the word for hard labour.
Dative, not the genitive ἐν μέσῳ τοῦ παραδείσου that classical Greek would want. The construction is a Hebraism; Rahlfs prints it as it stands.

reading: and sprang up from — one completed act seen whole, not a process observed in progress — [[the God|he who is God definitively, the one the article marks out, the known and the only]] [[yet|yet, as yet, still, further, besides, moreover]] [[out of|out of, forth from, from]] [[the earth|the land, the dry ground, the terrestrial realm]] [[all|all, the whole, every, every single]] [[wood|wood, firewood, timber, a piece of wood, a post, a stick]] [[produced at the right season|produced at the right season, seasonable, timely, of the season, gathered in due season]] [[into|into, to, in, rest in]] [[seeing|seeing, the act of sight, a vision]] and [[beautiful|beautiful, beauteous, fair, good]] [[into|into, to, in, rest in]] [[meat|meat, eating, corrosion and rust]] and [[the wood|the wood, the timber, the piece of wood]] [[of the life|of the life, of the means of life and substance, of existence, of a way of life]] [[in middle|within, inside of, and by means of the middle, in the middle, the centre, mid, between two]] [[the park|the park, the garden of Eden, paradise]] and [[the wood|the wood, the timber, the piece of wood]] [[to know|to know, to be assured, to be versed in]] [[known|known, to be known]] [[of beautiful|of beautiful, of beauteous, of fair, of good]] and [[of toilsome|of toilsome, of painful, of grievous, of good-for-nothing, of bad and worthless, of wicked]].

greek: ποταμὸς δὲ ἐκπορεύεται ἐξ Εδεμ ποτίζειν τὸν παράδεισον· ἐκεῖθεν ἀφορίζεται εἰς τέσσαρας ἀρχάς.
hint: Two presents in a narrative of aorists: the river is still doing this.

notes.text: Both present, in the middle of a past narrative: the river *goes out* and *is divided*, not *went* and *was*. The tense makes the geography contemporary with whoever is reading.

Middle Liddell files the deponent under its active, ἐκπορεύω, whose first gloss is *to make to go out, fetch out* — the active alone. The middle glosses it tags next, *to go out* and *forth, march out*, are this form, and the headword takes the first of those.

The word that opened Genesis and John: ἀρχή, *a beginning*, and also *rule, headship*. Here it is the head of a river — where a stream begins. The same noun, and the reading keeps the whole range so the connection stays visible.
Second occurrence in the chapter, so it stands bare: glossed once at 2:8.

reading: [[but|but, however, whereas, on the other hand]], [[a river|a river, a stream, a river-god]] [[goes out|goes out, goes forth, marches out]] [[out of|out of, forth from, from]] [[name:Εδεμ]] [[to give to drink|to give to drink, to water, to water the cattle]] [[the park|the park, the garden of Eden, paradise]]; [[from that place|from that place, thence, thereafter, next]] [[is marked off by boundaries|is marked off by boundaries, is marked off for itself, is distinguished and determined and defined, is set apart and separated]] [[into|into, to, in, rest in]] four [[beginnings|beginnings, origins, first causes, headships and rules and governing precedences]].

greek: ὄνομα τῷ ἑνὶ Φισων· οὗτος ὁ κυκλῶν πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν Ευιλατ, ἐκεῖ οὗ ἐστιν τὸ χρυσίον·
hint: No verb in the first clause: the Greek simply sets a name beside a thing.

notes.text: *A name to the one* — no copula, as Hebrew does it. The reading supplies nothing, because nothing is there to supply.
Articular present participle of κυκλόω, *to encircle, surround*: the one that goes round. Present, and so still going round.
The diminutive of χρυσός: Middle Liddell's first sense is *a piece of gold*, then gold as a substance, then coined money. The Greek names a nugget before it names the metal.

Both transliterated with no attempt at sense. Ευιλατ is Hebrew *Ḥăwîlâ*, usually connected with *ḥôl*, sand; Φισων is *Pîšôn*, of uncertain derivation, perhaps from *pûš*, to leap or spring. Neither river has been identified.

reading: [[a name|a name, fame, a mere name, a phrase and expression]] [[to the one|to the one, to a single one, to one alone]] [[name:Φισων]]; [[this|this, the nearer, what follows]] [[the one encircling|the one encircling, surrounding, moving in a circle, going round]] [[all|all, the whole, every, every single]] [[the earth|the land, the dry ground, the terrestrial realm]] [[name:Ευιλατ]], [[there|there, in that place]] where is [[the piece of gold|the piece of gold, gold, gold coin and money]];

names.gloss: (Φισων, from Hebrew Pîšôn, perhaps from pûš, "to leap, spring")
(Ευιλατ, from Hebrew Ḥăwîlâ, usually connected with ḥôl, "sand")

greek: τὸ δὲ χρυσίον τῆς γῆς ἐκείνης καλόν· καὶ ἐκεῖ ἐστιν ὁ ἄνθραξ καὶ ὁ λίθος ὁ πράσινος.
hint: Two stones, and the lexicon's first sense for one of them is charcoal.

notes.text: Middle Liddell gives one sense: *charcoal, coal*. The gem is named from the burning coal it looks like, which is how Latin *carbunculus*, a little coal, became the carbuncle. The Greek word says coal and the context says stone; the reading prints the word.

Middle Liddell has no πράσινος at all. LSJ gives *leek-green, light green*, from πράσον, a leek — and cites this very verse for the stone: λίθος π. = πρασῖτις. Its later sense, *the green faction*, belongs to the chariot-racing of the Circus and is not in play.
No copula again: *the gold of that land, beautiful*. And καλός is *beautiful* before it is *good* — the judgement on the gold is aesthetic first.

reading: [[but|but, however, whereas, on the other hand]], [[the piece of gold|the piece of gold, gold, gold coin and money]] [[of the earth|of the land, of the dry ground, of the terrestrial realm]] [[of that|of that, of the one there, of the more remote]] [[beautiful|beautiful, beauteous, fair, good]]; and [[there|there, in that place]] is [[the charcoal|the charcoal, the coal]] and [[the stone|the stone, the precious stone, the marble]] [[the leek-green|the leek-green, the light green]].

greek: καὶ ὄνομα τῷ ποταμῷ τῷ δευτέρῳ Γηων· οὗτος ὁ κυκλῶν πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν Αἰθιοπίας.
hint: The Hebrew says Cush; the Greek says the land of the burnt faces.

notes.text: Hebrew *Kûš*, a region south of Egypt. [[flag]] The Greek does not transliterate it but substitutes a Greek word with a Greek etymology — Αἰθιοπία, from αἴθω, *to burn*, and ὤψ, *face*: the land of the sun-burnt. A translator's gloss has become the text, and the Hebrew name has disappeared.
Hebrew *Gîḥôn*, from *gîaḥ*, to burst or gush forth — a name for a spring that breaks out of the ground. Jerusalem's own spring carries the same name in 1 Kings 1:33.

reading: and [[a name|a name, fame, a mere name, a phrase and expression]] [[to the river|to the river, to the stream]] the second [[name:Γηων]]; [[this|this, the nearer, what follows]] [[the one encircling|the one encircling, surrounding, moving in a circle, going round]] [[all|all, the whole, every, every single]] [[the earth|the land, the dry ground, the terrestrial realm]] of [[name:Αἰθιοπίας]].

names.gloss: (Γηων, from Hebrew Gîḥôn, from gîaḥ, "to burst forth")
(Αἰθιοπίας, from αἴθω, "to burn", and ὤψ, "face"; Hebrew Kûš)

greek: καὶ ὁ ποταμὸς ὁ τρίτος Τίγρις· οὗτος ὁ πορευόμενος κατέναντι Ἀσσυρίων. ὁ δὲ ποταμὸς ὁ τέταρτος, οὗτος Εὐφράτης.
hint: Two of the four rivers are on any map; two are on none.

notes.text: Middle Liddell files πορεύομαι under the active πορεύω, whose sense I is marked *Act.* — *to make to go, carry, convey* — and cannot be this form. Sense II is marked *Pass. and Mid.*, and its first gloss is *to be driven or carried*, with *to go, walk, march* following. The middle is available to both, so nothing is skipped inside it and the headword takes its first translation. A river that is carried along is not a strained reading of a current.

The entry in Middle Liddell carries no translation at all: it reads *κατέναντι = κατεναντίον*, and the senses are the ones that entry gives — *over against, opposite, before*. A cross-reference followed, not a sense chosen.

Both are Greek forms of Old Persian names rather than of the Hebrew. The Hebrew has *Ḥiddeqel* and *Pĕrāt*; the Greek prints Τίγρις, from *tigrā*, an arrow, for the speed of the current, and Εὐφράτης, from *Ufrātu*. Two rivers that exist, after two that no one has found.
The Assyrians, named from Aššur — their god, their first city, and their land at once. Genitive plural: the river runs opposite *them*, not opposite the country.

reading: and [[the river|the river, the stream, the river-god]] the third [[name:Τίγρις]]; [[this|this, the nearer, what follows]] [[the one being driven|the one being driven, being carried, going, walking, marching, going across and passing]] [[over against|over against, opposite, before]] [[name:Ἀσσυρίων]]. [[but|but, however, whereas, on the other hand]], [[the river|the river, the stream, the river-god]] the fourth, [[this|this, the nearer, what follows]] [[name:Εὐφράτης]].

names.gloss: (Τίγρις, from Old Persian tigrā, "arrow", for its swiftness; Hebrew Ḥiddeqel)
(Ἀσσυρίων, the Assyrians, from Aššur — their god, their city, and their land)
(Εὐφράτης, from Old Persian Ufrātu; Hebrew Pĕrāt)

greek: Καὶ ἔλαβεν κύριος ὁ θεὸς τὸν ἄνθρωπον, ὃν ἔπλασεν, καὶ ἔθετο αὐτὸν ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ ἐργάζεσθαι αὐτὸν καὶ φυλάσσειν.
hint: The man is put in the garden to do the two things the garden needs.

notes.text: αὐτόν is masculine and refers to παράδεισος, not to the man: he is to work *it*. English *it* hides the agreement; the Greek cannot be misread.

φυλάσσω opens at *to keep watch and ward, keep guard* — a sentry's word, used of garrisons and of watching by night. What the garden needs is not only cultivation but a guard, and the verb says so before it says *keep*.
Still ὁ ἄνθρωπος here, *the man*. The name does not arrive until the next verse, and the Greek keeps the common noun until then.

reading: And [[took|took, received, took hold of and grasped and seized]] — one completed act seen whole, not a process observed in progress — [[lord|lord, master, the one having power and authority over]] [[the God|he who is God definitively, the one the article marks out, the known and the only]] [[the man|the man, the human being, mankind]], whom [[formed|formed, moulded, shaped, put into a certain form]], and [[set|set, put, placed, planted, laid]] him [[in the park|within, inside of, and by means of the park, the garden of Eden, paradise]] [[to work|to work, to labour, to work at and make and build, to do and perform and accomplish]] it and [[to keep watch and ward|to keep watch and ward, to keep guard, to watch and guard and keep and defend]].

greek: καὶ ἐνετείλατο κύριος ὁ θεὸς τῷ Αδαμ λέγων Ἀπὸ παντὸς ξύλου τοῦ ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ βρώσει φάγῃ,
hint: The first words spoken to the man are a permission, not a prohibition.

notes.text: The name enters, and the Greek prints it bare — Αδαμ, indeclinable, with the article carrying the case. Hebrew *ʾādām* is the common noun *man*, from *ʾădāmâ*, the ground he was formed from; Greek keeps the sound and loses the pun, which is why the gloss carries it.

A dative noun before its own verb: *with eating you shall eat*. It renders the Hebrew infinitive absolute, which intensifies — *you may freely eat* — by a construction Greek does not have and so imitates word for word. The reading keeps the imitation rather than smoothing it to an adverb.
Capitalised because it opens direct speech, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in this verse's `speech` field so the checks do not take it for a proper name.

reading: and [[enjoined|enjoined, commanded]] — one completed act seen whole, not a process observed in progress — [[lord|lord, master, the one having power and authority over]] [[the God|he who is God definitively, the one the article marks out, the known and the only]] to [[name:Αδαμ]] [[saying|saying, speaking, declaring, calling by name, telling]] [[from|from, away from, far from, apart from]] [[all|all, the whole, every, every single]] [[of wood|of wood, of timber, of a piece of wood]] the [[in the park|within, inside of, and by means of the park, the garden of Eden, paradise]] [[with meat|with meat, with eating]] [[you will eat|you will eat, you will eat of]],

greek: ἀπὸ δὲ τοῦ ξύλου τοῦ γινώσκειν καλὸν καὶ πονηρόν, οὐ φάγεσθε ἀπʼ αὐτοῦ· ᾗ δʼ ἂν ἡμέρᾳ φάγητε ἀπʼ αὐτοῦ, θανάτῳ ἀποθανεῖσθε.
hint: Singular in 2:16, plural here: the command is given to one and binds two.

notes.text: A different verb from 2:9. There the tree is τοῦ εἰδέναι, from οἶδα — *to know*, the knowledge one simply has. Here it is τοῦ γινώσκειν, from γινώσκω — *to learn to know, to perceive, to mark*, knowledge that is come by. The same tree, named twice, with two words English renders alike.
All plural, where 2:16 had the singular φάγῃ. The permission is addressed to the man alone; the prohibition is already addressed to more than one, several verses before the woman is made.
The same construction as βρώσει φάγῃ, and the same Hebrew idiom behind it: *with death you shall die*. Not *you shall surely die* — that is the idiom resolved; the Greek leaves it standing.
Elided before a vowel, three times. The mark is printed in Rahlfs and written here as U+02BC, the character the SBLGNT uses, so one convention covers both testaments.

reading: [[but|but, however, whereas, on the other hand]], [[from|from, away from, far from, apart from]] [[of the wood|of the wood, of the timber, of the piece of wood]] [[to learn to know|to learn to know, to perceive, to mark, to learn, to discern and distinguish]] [[beautiful|beautiful, beauteous, fair, good]] and [[toilsome|toilsome, painful, grievous, good-for-nothing, bad and worthless, wicked]], not [[you will eat|you will eat, you will eat of]] [[from|from, away from, far from, apart from]] it; in which [[day|the day, the day-break, the time]] ever [[you may eat|you may eat, you may eat of]] [[from|from, away from, far from, apart from]] it, [[with death|with death, with the death threatened, with the sentence of death]] [[you will die off|you will die off, you will die, you will be put to death, you will be slain]].

greek: Καὶ εἶπεν κύριος ὁ θεός Οὐ καλὸν εἶναι τὸν ἄνθρωπον μόνον· ποιήσωμεν αὐτῷ βοηθὸν κατʼ αὐτόν.
hint: The first thing called not good, in a chapter that has called everything else beautiful.

notes.text: καλός is *beautiful* before it is *good*, so what is denied here is in the first place a fitness, a rightness of form. Against the refrain of chapter 1 — καὶ εἶδεν ὁ θεὸς ὅτι καλόν — this is the single negation.
First person plural subjunctive: *let us make*, as at 1:26. The Greek reproduces the Hebrew plural exactly and adds nothing to explain it.

βοηθός is an entry that opens as an adjective, *assisting, auxiliary*; the first noun sense is *an assistant*. The word is used in the Septuagint of God himself as the helper of Israel, so it carries no implication of lesser rank. κατά with the accusative — the same preposition as κατὰ ἀνατολάς — renders Hebrew *kĕnegdô*, *corresponding to him*.

reading: And [[said|said, spoke, declared, called by name, told]] [[lord|lord, master, the one having power and authority over]] [[the God|he who is God definitively, the one the article marks out, the known and the only]] not [[beautiful|beautiful, beauteous, fair, good]] [[to be|to be, to exist]] [[the man|the man, the human being, mankind]] [[alone|alone, left alone, forsaken and solitary, only]]; [[let us make|let us make, let us do, let us produce and create]] to him [[an assistant|an assistant, one assisting and auxiliary]] [[down|down, downwards, down from, down upon, over, upon]] him.

greek: καὶ ἔπλασεν ὁ θεὸς ἔτι ἐκ τῆς γῆς πάντα τὰ θηρία τοῦ ἀγροῦ καὶ πάντα τὰ πετεινὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ καὶ ἤγαγεν αὐτὰ πρὸς τὸν Αδαμ ἰδεῖν, τί καλέσει αὐτά, καὶ πᾶν, ὃ ἐὰν ἐκάλεσεν αὐτὸ Αδαμ ψυχὴν ζῶσαν, τοῦτο ὄνομα αὐτοῦ.
hint: God brings them to see what the man will call them, and whatever he calls them is what they are.

notes.text: Aorist infinitive of ὁράω: God brings the animals *to see* what the man would call them. The subject of the seeing is left open — it can be God's seeing or the man's — and Greek does not resolve it.

The same phrase used of the man at 2:7, here of every animal. The Greek makes no distinction of kind between them at this point, and a version that renders it *living soul* of the man and *living creature* of the beasts has made one.

*And God formed yet* — the animals are formed after the man, as chapter 2 has it, where chapter 1 has them before. The Greek ἔτι, *still, further*, marks the continuation plainly rather than smoothing the order; some English versions render a pluperfect, *had formed*, which the Greek does not say.
Twice here, both bare: glossed once at 2:16.

reading: and [[formed|formed, moulded, shaped, put into a certain form]] — one completed act seen whole, not a process observed in progress — [[the God|he who is God definitively, the one the article marks out, the known and the only]] [[yet|yet, as yet, still, further, besides, moreover]] [[out of|out of, forth from, from]] [[the earth|the land, the dry ground, the terrestrial realm]] [[all|all, the whole, every, every single]] [[the wild animals|the wild animals, the beasts, the savage beasts, the game]] [[of field|of field, of lands, of a farm, of the country]] and [[all|all, the whole, every, every single]] [[the winged fowl|the winged fowl, the birds, the able to fly and full fledged]] [[of heaven|of heaven, of the vault, of the firmament and the sky]] and [[led|led, carried, conveyed, brought, marched]] them [[toward|toward, facing, oriented to, in living motion and address toward]] [[name:Αδαμ]] [[to see|to see, to perceive, to behold, to look at]], what [[he will call|he will call, he will summon, he will call to himself, he will invite]] them, and [[all|all, the whole, every, every single]], which if [[called|called, summoned, called to himself, invited]] it [[name:Αδαμ]] [[breath|breath, the life, the spirit, the ghost, the departed soul]] [[living|living, alive, in full life and strength, fresh, strong]], [[this|this, the nearer, what follows]] [[a name|a name, fame, a mere name, a phrase and expression]] of it.

greek: Καὶ ἐκάλεσεν Αδαμ ὀνόματα πᾶσιν τοῖς κτήνεσιν καὶ πᾶσι τοῖς πετεινοῖς τοῦ οὐρανοῦ καὶ πᾶσι τοῖς θηρίοις τοῦ ἀγροῦ, τῷ δὲ Αδαμ οὐχ εὑρέθη βοηθὸς ὅμοιος αὐτῷ. —
hint: The naming is finished, and the thing it was for has not been found.

notes.text: κτῆνος opens at *flocks and herds* — property, from κτάομαι, to acquire. The domestic animals are named by their belonging to someone, where θηρία are named by their wildness.
Aorist passive: *was not found*. Not *there was none* — the Greek reports a search that came to nothing, which is what makes the verse the hinge of the chapter.
*Like to him*, where 2:18 had κατʼ αὐτόν, *corresponding to him*. The Greek uses two different phrases for the one Hebrew *kĕnegdô*, and the reading keeps both rather than levelling them.
Rahlfs prints a dash after αὐτῷ, marking the break before the sleep falls. It is the editor's paragraph mark rather than a word of the text, so it stands in the Greek line and not in the reading.

reading: And [[called|called, summoned, called to himself, invited]] — one completed act seen whole, not a process observed in progress — [[name:Αδαμ]] [[names|names, fames, mere names, phrases and expressions]] [[to all|to all, to the whole, to every, to every single]] [[to the flocks and herds|to the flocks and herds, to the single beast, to the ox, to the sheep, to the beast for riding]] and [[to all|to all, to the whole, to every, to every single]] [[to the winged fowl|to the winged fowl, to the birds, to the able to fly and full fledged]] [[of heaven|of heaven, of the vault, of the firmament and the sky]] and [[to all|to all, to the whole, to every, to every single]] [[to the wild animals|to the wild animals, to the beasts, to the savage beasts, to the game]] [[of field|of field, of lands, of a farm, of the country]], [[but|but, however, whereas, on the other hand]] to [[name:Αδαμ]] not [[was found|was found, was found out, was discovered]] [[an assistant|an assistant, one assisting and auxiliary]] [[like|like, resembling, the same, all one, shared alike by both]] to him.

greek: καὶ ἐπέβαλεν ὁ θεὸς ἔκστασιν ἐπὶ τὸν Αδαμ, καὶ ὕπνωσεν· καὶ ἔλαβεν μίαν τῶν πλευρῶν αὐτοῦ καὶ ἀνεπλήρωσεν σάρκα ἀντʼ αὐτῆς.
hint: The word for the sleep is the word the New Testament uses for a vision.

notes.text: Not sleep but ἔκστασις — a standing outside oneself. Middle Liddell gives it as *any displacement: entrancement, astonishment*, and then *a trance*. It is the word used of Peter on the roof in Acts 10:10 and of the women at the tomb in Mark 16:8. The Hebrew *tardēmâ* is a deep sleep; the Greek makes it a displacement of the mind.

The lexicon's first sense is transitive and causative, *to put to sleep*; *to fall asleep, sleep* is its second. The Septuagint uses the active intransitively here — he slept — and the headword keeps the lexicon's order with the note carrying the usage.
πλευρά is *a rib*, and also *the side* — of a body, an army, a building, a page. Greek does not choose, and neither does the reading. *One of his ribs* and *one of his sides* are the same phrase.
ἀναπληρόω is *to fill up*, to make good a deficiency — used of filling a gap in a line of troops or paying a debt in full. The flesh does not replace the rib so much as make the place whole again.

reading: and [[threw|threw, cast upon, laid on, affixed, added]] [[the God|he who is God definitively, the one the article marks out, the known and the only]] [[any displacement|any displacement, entrancement, astonishment, a trance]] [[upon|upon, on, in, at, near]] [[name:Αδαμ]], and [[put to sleep|put to sleep, fell asleep, slept]]; and [[took|took, received, took hold of and grasped and seized]] [[one|one, a single one, one alone]] [[of ribs|of ribs, of the ribs and the side, of one side, of the page]] of him and [[filled up|filled up, made up and supplied, filled, paid in full]] [[flesh|flesh, the flesh, muscles, the body, man's nature generally]] [[over against|over against, opposite, instead, in the place of, as good as]] her.

greek: καὶ ᾠκοδόμησεν κύριος ὁ θεὸς τὴν πλευράν, ἣν ἔλαβεν ἀπὸ τοῦ Αδαμ, εἰς γυναῖκα καὶ ἤγαγεν αὐτὴν πρὸς τὸν Αδαμ.
hint: The verb is the one used of building a house.

notes.text: οἰκοδομέω is built from οἶκος and δέμω: *to build a house*, which Middle Liddell gives as its first sense before the general *to build*. The rib is built into a woman with the verb used of masonry, and the Hebrew *bānâ* does the same.
εἰς of result again, as at 2:7 where the man came to be εἰς ψυχὴν ζῶσαν. The rib is built *into* a woman: the preposition marks what it became.
πρός with the accusative, the directional preposition of John 1:1 — toward, facing, in address toward. She is not delivered *to* him but brought *facing* him.

reading: and [[built a house|built a house, built, built for himself]] — one completed act seen whole, not a process observed in progress — [[lord|lord, master, the one having power and authority over]] [[the God|he who is God definitively, the one the article marks out, the known and the only]] [[the rib|the rib, the ribs and the side, one side, the page]], which [[took|took, received, took hold of and seized]] [[from|from, away from, far from, apart from]] [[name:Αδαμ]], [[into|into, to, in, rest in]] [[a woman|a woman, a mistress and lady, a wife and spouse, a mortal woman]] and [[led|led, carried, conveyed, brought, marched]] her [[toward|toward, facing, oriented to, in living motion and address toward]] [[name:Αδαμ]].

greek: καὶ εἶπεν Αδαμ Τοῦτο νῦν ὀστοῦν ἐκ τῶν ὀστέων μου καὶ σὰρξ ἐκ τῆς σαρκός μου· αὕτη κληθήσεται γυνή, ὅτι ἐκ τοῦ ἀνδρὸς αὐτῆς ἐλήμφθη αὕτη.
hint: The Hebrew puns and the Greek cannot.

notes.text: The Hebrew turns on a pun: *ʾiššâ*, woman, from *ʾîš*, man. [[flag]] Greek γυνή and ἀνήρ are unrelated words, and the reason clause — *she shall be called woman, because she was taken out of her man* — loses the thing that made it a reason. The Greek keeps the sentence and drops its hinge; no English version can recover it either, because English *woman* and *man* only look related.

ἀνήρ, not ἄνθρωπος: the male, against the human being of 2:7 and 2:15. This is the first time the chapter distinguishes them, and both would be *man* in English, which is why the notes must say which is which.
The Attic contraction of ὀστέον. Middle Liddell has the entry but tags no usable translation in it — only *the*, sliced out of a quoted phrase — so the sense here is LSJ's, *bone*.
Neuter — *this thing*, not *this woman* — and capitalised because it opens direct speech; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take it for a name.

reading: and [[said|said, spoke, declared, called by name, told]] [[name:Αδαμ]] [[this|this, the nearer, what follows]] [[now|now, even now, just now]] [[bone|bone, the bones of the dead]] [[out of|out of, forth from, from]] [[of the bones|of the bones, of the bones of the dead]] of me and [[flesh|flesh, the flesh, muscles, the body, man's nature generally]] [[out of|out of, forth from, from]] [[of the flesh|of the flesh, of the muscles, of the body]] of me; [[this|this, the nearer, what follows]] [[she will be called|she will be called, she will be summoned, she will be invited]] [[a woman|a woman, a mistress and lady, a wife and spouse, a mortal woman]], [[that|that, seeing that, although, for that, because, inasmuch as]] [[out of|out of, forth from, from]] [[of the man|of the man, of the man in the prime of life]] of her [[was taken|was taken, was received, was taken hold of and seized]] [[this|this, the nearer, what follows]].

greek: ἕνεκεν τούτου καταλείψει ἄνθρωπος τὸν πατέρα αὐτοῦ καὶ τὴν μητέρα αὐτοῦ καὶ προσκολληθήσεται πρὸς τὴν γυναῖκα αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν.
hint: The verse quoted in Matthew, Mark, First Corinthians and Ephesians — and οἱ δύο is in none of the Hebrew.

notes.text: *The two* is not in the Hebrew, which reads only *and they shall become one flesh*. [[flag]] The Greek supplies the number, and every New Testament quotation of the verse — Matthew 19:5, Mark 10:8, 1 Corinthians 6:16, Ephesians 5:31 — quotes the Greek with it. A phrase added by translators became the text the apostles argued from, which is the whole case for reading the Old Testament in Greek.
προσκολλάω is *to glue on*: κόλλα is glue, and English *collagen* and *protocol* are its relatives. Future passive in form — he *will be glued* — where English makes it active, *shall cleave*.
Anarthrous and general: *a human being*, not the man of the story. The verse steps out of the narrative into a rule.

reading: [[on account of|on account of, for the sake of, because of, for, as far as regards]] [[of this|of this, of the nearer, of what follows]] [[will leave behind|will leave behind, will leave behind him, will leave as an inheritance]] [[man|a man, a human being]] [[the father|the father, the grandfather]] of him and [[the mother|the mother, the dam, the source]] of him and [[will be glued on|will be glued on, will stick, will cleave to]] [[toward|toward, facing, oriented to, in living motion and address toward]] [[the woman|the woman, the mistress and lady, the wife and spouse]] of him, and will be the two [[into|into, to, in, rest in]] [[flesh|flesh, the flesh, muscles, the body]] [[one|one, a single one, one alone]].

greek: καὶ ἦσαν οἱ δύο γυμνοί, ὅ τε Αδαμ καὶ ἡ γυνὴ αὐτοῦ, καὶ οὐκ ᾐσχύνοντο.
hint: The last verse of the chapter, and the last before everything changes.

notes.text: Imperfect, middle or passive — the two share one form in this tense. αἰσχύνω's active senses are *to make ugly, disfigure, mar* and *to dishonour*; the first numbered sense open to this voice is *to be ashamed, feel shame*, and that is the one taken. The imperfect holds it open: they were not, and kept on not being, ashamed.

γυμνός runs from *naked* through *unarmed* to *uncovered* — the word behind *gymnasium*, where the exercise was done stripped. It is not only a state of dress but of defencelessness, and the next chapter turns on that.
τε couples closely: *both Adam and his wife*, taken as one pair rather than two parties. Rahlfs prints the article ὅ before the indeclinable name.

reading: and were, and kept on being as a standing and continuing condition and not a momentary one, the two [[naked|naked, unclad, unarmed, uncovered, stripped of]], both [[name:Αδαμ]] and [[the woman|the woman, the mistress and lady, the wife and spouse]] of him, and not [[were being ashamed|were being ashamed, were feeling shame, were being dishonoured]].
